pharm: Mutant isocitrate dehydrogenase-2 (IDH2) inhibitor; lowers oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) and restores myeloid differentiation
tags: Relapsed or refractory AML with IDH2 mutation
Noninfectious leukocytosis and tumor lysis syndrome
quick: Take with or without food at the same time each day
Can cause fetal harm; avoid - use effective contraception
Do not breastfeed during and for 2 months after the last dose
No adjustment defined; monitor tumor lysis labs and for differentiation syndrome
No adjustment defined; monitor bilirubin; reduce dose for sustained isolated hyperbilirubinemia
No specific interaction; limit due to additive hepatic effects
Differentiation syndrome signs, WBC, bilirubin, tumor lysis labs, pregnancy status
summary: Enasidenib (Idhifa) is an oral mutant IDH2 inhibitor for adults with relapsed or refractory acute myeloid leukemia with an IDH2 mutation detected by an FDA-approved test. The dose is 100 mg once daily with or without food until progression or unacceptable toxicity. It carries a boxed warning for differentiation syndrome (about 14% of patients, onset day 1 to 5 months, potentially fatal), managed with corticosteroids, hemodynamic monitoring, and hydroxyurea if leukocytosis is present. Other key risks are noninfectious leukocytosis, tumor lysis syndrome, hyperbilirubinemia, and embryo-fetal toxicity.
indications: Treatment of adults with relapsed or refractory acute myeloid leukemia (AML) with an isocitrate dehydrogenase-2 (IDH2) mutation as detected by an FDA-approved test

dosage.c: Relapsed or refractory AML with IDH2 mutation
dosage.n: Continue until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity; assess response per oncology follow-up
dosage.t: Once daily, with or without food

dosage.d: Start systemic corticosteroids promptly with hemodynamic monitoring; taper only after resolution
dosage.n: Differentiation syndrome occurred in about 14% of patients, as early as day 1 and up to 5 months after starting, with or without hyperleukocytosis; hold enasidenib if severe pulmonary symptoms or renal dysfunction require intensive care

dosage.d: Treat with hydroxyurea per institutional practice; taper only after leukocytosis improves
dosage.n: Consider holding enasidenib if leukocytosis does not improve promptly; leukapheresis may be used if clinically indicated

dosage.d: For bilirubin above 3 times the upper limit of normal lasting more than 2 weeks without transaminase rise, reduce dose to 50 mg once daily
dosage.n: Resume 100 mg daily if bilirubin falls to 2 times the upper limit or less; discontinue if bilirubin stays elevated with transaminase rise

admin: Take 100 mg by mouth once daily, with or without food, at about the same time each day
Swallow tablets whole with water; do not split, crush, or chew
Continue until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity

If differentiation syndrome is suspected (fever, dyspnea, hypoxia, pulmonary infiltrates, rash, edema, rapid weight gain, hypotension), seek urgent care; treatment is systemic corticosteroids with hemodynamic monitoring
Obtain baseline pregnancy status, blood counts, bilirubin, electrolytes, and tumor lysis labs; monitor leukocyte count for noninfectious leukocytosis
moa: Enasidenib is a small-molecule inhibitor of mutant isocitrate dehydrogenase-2 (IDH2). Mutant IDH2 produces the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), which impairs histone and DNA demethylation and blocks myeloid differentiation. Enasidenib lowers 2-HG, restores differentiation, and reduces leukemic blasts in IDH2-mutated relapsed or refractory AML. Differentiation of blasts underlies both response and the differentiation syndrome risk.

absolute: Known serious hypersensitivity to enasidenib or any excipient
monitor: Signs of differentiation syndrome (fever, dyspnea, hypoxia, rash, weight gain, edema, hypotension)
White blood cell count for noninfectious leukocytosis
Bilirubin and tumor lysis labs (uric acid, potassium, phosphate, calcium, creatinine)
relative: Pre-existing hyperbilirubinemia or Gilbert syndrome (drug raises bilirubin)
Risk factors for tumor lysis syndrome (high leukemic burden)
Concomitant drugs that raise bilirubin or are sensitive OATP1B1/1B3, CYP, or transporter substrates

preg: Based on its mechanism and animal findings, enasidenib can cause fetal harm including embryofetal mortality and growth delay. Verify pregnancy status before starting. Advise females of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment and for 2 months after the last dose; advise males with female partners of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment and for 2 months after the last dose.
lact: There are no data on enasidenib in human milk or its effects on the breastfed infant or milk production. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions, advise women not to breastfeed during treatment and for 2 months after the last dose.
renal: No dose adjustment is defined for renal impairment. Monitor renal function and tumor lysis labs, especially during differentiation syndrome or leukocytosis, and manage volume and uric acid per standard care.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is defined for hepatic impairment, but enasidenib commonly raises bilirubin (including via UGT1A1 inhibition), which can confound liver assessment. Monitor bilirubin and transaminases; dose-reduce per labeling for isolated sustained hyperbilirubinemia and hold or discontinue if transaminases also rise.

interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction is described; limit alcohol because of additive liver and constitutional effects.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor CBC with differential (WBC for leukocytosis), bilirubin and transaminases, tumor lysis labs (uric acid, electrolytes, creatinine), and pregnancy status.
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; no clinically significant food effect requiring dose change.
major: Sensitive substrates of CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, or CYP3A4 with a narrow therapeutic index - enasidenib may alter their exposure; avoid combinations or monitor closely
OATP1B1, OATP1B3, BCRP, or P-gp substrates with a narrow therapeutic index (e.g., certain statins) - enasidenib may increase their exposure; monitor and reduce substrate dose as needed
minor: Gastric acid-reducing agents have no major described effect on dosing
moderate: Drugs that raise bilirubin or inhibit UGT1A1 - additive hyperbilirubinemia; monitor bilirubin
Hydroxyurea is used therapeutically for enasidenib-associated leukocytosis per labeling (beneficial interaction)

emergency: Fever with dyspnea, hypoxia, rash, rapid weight gain, swelling, or hypotension (differentiation syndrome) - seek emergency care
Very low urine output with muscle cramps, nausea, or confusion (tumor lysis syndrome)
Severe dyspnea, chest pain, or marked WBC rise with fever (leukocytosis complications)
rare: Severe drug-induced liver injury with transaminase elevation
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy-like neurologic events reported in class experience (evaluate new neurologic symptoms)
serious: Differentiation syndrome, which can be fatal (boxed warning)

monitoring: Signs and symptoms of differentiation syndrome from day 1 through at least 5 months after starting
Complete blood counts with differential for noninfectious leukocytosis
Bilirubin, transaminases, and tumor lysis labs (uric acid, potassium, phosphate, calcium, creatinine)
Pregnancy status before starting in females of reproductive potential
counsel: This drug carries a boxed warning for differentiation syndrome, which can be fatal: report fever, trouble breathing, rash, swelling, rapid weight gain, or dizziness right away, even months after starting
Take one tablet once a day with or without food; if you miss a dose, vomit, or have diarrhea after a dose, take the next dose at the regular time - do not double up
Report yellowing of skin or eyes (bilirubin rise is common but needs evaluation), severe nausea or vomiting, muscle cramps, or very low urine output

Use effective contraception during treatment and for 2 months after the last dose (both female patients and males with partners who could become pregnant); do not breastfeed during and for 2 months after the last dose
Tell your team about all medicines, especially statins, hormonal contraceptives, and drugs moved by liver transporters
pk: 2-HG reduction within days; hematologic responses develop over weeks to months
Median plasma Tmax about 4 hours after oral dosing
Mean terminal half-life about 137 hours (about 6 days)
Steady state reached in about 29 days with once-daily dosing; drug persists for weeks after stopping
Store at 20-25 C (excursions 15-30 C permitted); keep in original container
pearls: Boxed warning: differentiation syndrome in about 14% of patients, potentially fatal - start corticosteroids and hemodynamic monitoring at the first suspicion, with or without leukocytosis
Noninfectious leukocytosis is common - treat promptly with hydroxyurea and hold drug if severe or unresponsive
Hyperbilirubinemia is common (partly UGT1A1 inhibition) - distinguish isolated bilirubin rise (dose-reduce) from transaminase-associated injury
Broad transporter and CYP interaction profile - review statins and narrow therapeutic index substrates before starting
Very long half-life with steady state over about 29 days - adverse effects and contraception need extend for 2 months after stopping
missed: If a dose is missed, vomited, or followed by diarrhea, take the next dose at the regularly scheduled time the next day. Do not take two doses together to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: There is no specific antidote for enasidenib overdose. Manage with supportive care, including monitoring for differentiation syndrome, leukocytosis, tumor lysis abnormalities, and hepatic effects, with prolonged observation given the long half-life. Contact Poison Help (1-800-222-1222).
